To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the security of property-preserving encrypted database columns is not as high as previously thought, and the security of these columns is significantly lower in a steady-state than in a cold-start scenario.

(i) the state-of-the-art property-preserving encrypted database systems provide little security against inference attacks; (ii) the security of these systems can be significantly improved by applying the appropriate security measures; and (iii) these systems can be used to protect sensitive data in the cloud if they are used correctly.

(i) OPE and DTE provide only a limited amount of privacy; (ii) the security of OPE and DPE is sensitive to the specific encryption parameters; and (iii) the security of an EDB system is sensitive to the application’s query patterns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental question about EDB systems: How much information about the plaintext database can be recovered from its encrypted representation?
understanding the concrete security of state-of-the-art property-preserving encryption-based EDB systems.
the question of whether property-preserving encryption can be used to protect sensitive data in the cloud.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
property-preserving encryption (PPE) schemes are not secure enough to protect sensitive data in the presence of auxiliary information.
the security of EDB systems that rely on DTE and OPE schemes is not as high as it was previously thought to be.
the security of the state-of-the-art property-preserving EDB systems has been seriously overstated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the state-of-the-art property-preserving EDB systems are not secure against inference attacks.
the state of the art EDB systems are not as secure as one would expect, especially in the steady state where enough encryption layers are peeled to permit the applications to run their queries.
, while property-preserving encryption is a powerful technique that can enable many applications, it is not a panacea for secure database outsourcing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the concrete security of existing EDB systems is much weaker than their designers intended.
the security provided by property-preserving encryption in practice is far weaker than the security provided by the encryption schemes in theory.
the security provided by property-preserving encryption is not adequate for protecting sensitive data in practice, and we call for more secure EDB systems that provide stronger privacy guarantees.
